full_judgment:
15. The petitioner was apprehensive that the respondent No.3 might encash the bank guarantees numbered 1103190063 dated 11-4-2019 and 1103220067 dated 26-4-2022 at any time. As such, the petitioner filed Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 33 of 2024 under section 7(A) of the Arbitration Act, 2001, before the learned District Judge, Dhaka, seeking an injunction to restrain the opposite parties from encashing the performance guarantees. The learned District judge, Dhaka, admitted the case on 23-4-2024 but did not issue interim order, instead giving the opposite parties a 15-day show cause notice. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the order dated 23-4-2024, the Petitioner filed Civil Revision No. 1839 of 2024 before the Hon'ble High Court Division. The High Court Division subsequently passed an order of status quo for two months regarding the Performance Guarantees. The petitioner also served a Notice of Arbitration on respondent Nos. 4 and 6 on 27-6-2024. 

 18. The respondent No. 2 invoked RIP, বিদ্যুৎ ও জ্বালানীর দ্রুত সরবরাহ বৃদ্ধি (বিশেষ বিধান) আইন, ২০১০ in directing the respondent No.3 (BPC) to cancel the contract with the respondent No.4, NKFTCL. However, the Act of 2010 does not contain any provision which empowers Government/Ministry to cancel a contract, substantial performance of which has already been carried out. Infact, sections 5 to 7 of the Act of 2010 clearly manifest that a technical processing committee has to be formed to submit proposal regarding “ক্রয় এবং বিনিয়োগ পরিকল্পনা বা প্রস্তাব” which would eventually be submitted before অর্থনৈতিক বিষয় বা সরকারি ক্রয় সংক্রান্ত মন্ত্রিসভা কমিটি for approval. In the instant case (as evident from the impugned notice) neither any technical processing committee was formed nor any proposal was submitted before the অর্থনৈতিক বিষয় বা সরকারি ক্রয় সংক্রান্ত মন্ত্রিসভা কমিটি nor there has been any approval from অর্থনৈতিক বিষয় বা সরকারি ক্রয় সংক্রান্ত মন্ত্রিসভা কমিটি recommending cancellation of the project contract. 

 26. Mr. Ahsanul Karim, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that respondent No.2 invoked বিদ্যুৎ ও জ্বালানীর দ্রুত সরবরাহ বৃদ্ধি (বিশেষ বিধান) আইন, ২০১০ in directing BPC to cancel the contract with NKFTCL; however, the Act of 2010 does not contain any provision which empowers the Government or a statutory corporation such as BPC to cancel a contract, substantial performance of which has already been carried out. Infact, sections 5 to 7 of the Act of 2010 clearly manifest that a technical processing committee has to be formed to submit a proposal regarding “ক্রয় এবং বিনিয়োগ পরিকল্পনা বা প্রস্তাব” which would eventually be submitted before অর্থনৈতিক বিষয় বা সরকারি ক্রয় সংক্রান্ত মন্ত্রিসভা কমিটি for approval. In the instant case, as evident from the impugned .notice dated 26-6-2024 neither any technical processing committee was formed nor any proposal was submitted before the অর্থনৈতিক বিষয় বা সরকারি ক্রয় সংক্রান্ত মন্ত্রিসভা কমিটি nor there has been any approval from অর্থনৈতিক বিষয় বা সরকারি ক্রয় সংক্রান্ত মন্ত্রিসভা কমিটি recommending cancellation of the project contract. 

 32. Mr. Karim further submits that as evident from the impugned directive [Annexure G to the writ petition] and Government notification dated 9-10-2017 [Annexure B to the writ petition], the contract for the Project in question is rooted in বিদ্যুৎ ও জ্বালানীর দ্রুত সরবরাহ বৃদ্ধি (বিশেষ বিধান) আইন, ২০১০ since sections 4 to 7 of the Act of 2010 expressly empowers Statutory Bodies such as BPC to nominate/propose contractor for circulation and transpiration of fuel oil before ECNEC (Executive Committee of the National Economic Council). In the instant case, the respondent No.1-3 in exercise o fits power rooted in বিদ্যুৎ ও জ্বালানীর দ্রুত সরবরাহ বৃদ্ধি (বিশেষ বিধান) আইন, ২০১০ entered into a contract with EPC (Engineering, Procurement and Construction) contractor, the respondent No.4, NKFTCL. 

 34. In support of the submissions, the learned Advocate of the petitioner, referred to the cases of Acqua Foods Limited and another vs Controller of Imports and Exports and others, reported in 49 DLR 498; Managing Director, Dhaka WASA Superior Builders and Engineers Ltd, reported in 51 DLR (AD) 56; IT, Dacca vs Mr. AW Mallik and others, reported in 20 DLR (SC) 229; Dr. Syed Matiur Rob being dead his heirs Shamsun Nahar & Others vs Bangladesh and others, reported in 9 BLD (AD) 52; Ministry of Industries, Nationalized Industries Division vs Saleh Ahmed & Another and Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation vs Saleh Ahmed and others, reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 91; Amir Hossain Sowdagar vs Md. Harunur Rashid and others, reported in 65 DLR (AD) 130; Pir Mohammad Farid Jan & others vs Colonisation Officer, Sukkur Barrage, Hyderabad and others, reported in 17 DLR SC 181; ABB India Limited vs Power Grid Company of Bangladesh Ltd and others, reported in 73 DLR 362; Privatization Board vs AK Fazlul Hug and another, reported in 55 DLR (AD) 11. 

 35. Conversely, Mr. Ashraful Hadi, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No.3 by filing an affidavit-in-opposition, submits that the instant writ petition is not maintainable since that the impugned notice dated 26-6-2024 issued by the respondent No.2 is an inter-ministerial or inter department communication not addressed to the petitioner and the petitioner was not a party to it and, hence, the petitioner being a sub-sub-contractor does not have any locus standi, The impugned notice is a memo of approval purely related to the commercial contracts, and, as such, no writ lies against any alleged violation of such commercial contracts. The appropriate remedy lies in a civil jurisdiction, but not in a writ jurisdiction. The petitioner has admittedly filed several miscellaneous arbitration cases for the appointment of an arbitrator under section 12 of the Arbitration Act, 2001, and for ad-interim status quo under section 7Ka of the Arbitration Act, 2001. 

 37. Mr. Hadi further submits that the petitioner has alternative and efficacious remedy to address any of its grievance by way of filing civil proceedings or pursuing arbitration proceedings, which forums have already been availed and being continued by the petitioner by way of filing Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No.407 of 2024 under section 12 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 for appointment of arbitrator impleading the respondent No.3 as the pro-forma opposite parties, and also by filing Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No.33 of 2024 under section 7Ka of the Arbitration Act, 2001 and Civil Revision No.1839 of 2024. Thus, if the petitioner has any claim under its contract with the respondent No.4, it may raise such a claim before a duly constituted arbitral tribunal, and hence, the petitioner is not entitled to any relief under the instant writ petition and for the further reason that the matter involves disputed questions of fact and needs examination of evidence to adjudicate properly. 

 41. In support of the submissions, the learned Advocate of the respondent No.3, referred to the cases of Nazrul Islam (Md) and another vs Government of Bangladesh and others, reported in 58 DLR 431; Md. Mobarak Hossain vs Government of the Bangladesh and others, reported in 19 BLT (HCD) 54; NG Projects vs Vinod Kumar Jain and others, reported in AIR 2022 SC 1531; KS Rashid and Son vs The Income Tax Investigation Commission and others, reported in AIR 1954 SC 207; KPM Builders Private Limited vs National Highways Authority of India and another, reported in 15 SCC 394; Raj Kumar Bahal vs Food Corporation of India and others, reported in AIR 1990 Raj 64; Government of Bangladesh vs Kazi Mofizul Haque, reported in 20 ADC 879; Superintendent Engineer, RHD Sylhet & Others vs Md. Eunus and Brother (Pvt) Ltd. [Along with Civil Appeal Nos. 245-250 of 20051, reported in 16 BLC (AD) 73; Bangladesh Power Development Board and others vs Md. Asaduzzaman Sikder, reported in 9 BLC (AD) 1. 

 42. Mr. Syed Ejaz Kabir, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No.1 by filing an affidavit-in-opposition, submits that the writ petition is not maintainable because the petitioner, a sub-sub-contractor, lacks locus standi. This is due to the impugned memo being an internal, inter-departmental communication, not addressed to or involving the petitioner. Crucially, there's no privity of contract between the petitioner and the main contract parties (Respondent No. 3 and the Bangladesh Navy), meaning the petitioner has no enforceable rights under those agreements. Furthermore, the memo concerns commercial contracts, for which civil jurisdiction or arbitration are the appropriate remedies, not a writ petition. The petitioner is already pursuing alternative and efficacious remedies through multiple arbitration cases and a civil revision, indicating the dispute involves questions of fact better resolved in those forums. The impugned memo from Respondent No. 2 is defended as legitimate, being an approval of Respondent No.3's proposals, not a dictation. The decision was based on valid reasons that the Respondent No.4's reliance on an incompetent sub-contractor (the petitioner) and an exorbitantly high revised proposal. This action was taken with bona fide intention to save government funds and ensure the timely completion of a critical project, suggesting a breach of contract by Respondent No. 4 and no wrongdoing by Respondent No. 3, and, as such, the rules issued in the instant writ petition are liable to be discharged. In support of his submission, he cited the cases of Superintendent Engineer, RHD Sylhet & Others vs Md. Eunus and Brother (Pvt) Ltd. (Along with Civil Appeal Nos.245-250 of 2005), reported in 16 BLC (AD) 73; Bangladesh Power Development Board and others vs Md. Asaduzzaman Sikder, reported in 9 BLC (AD) 1. 

 49. It further appears that the petitioner has initiated the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No.33 of 2024 on 22-1-2024 against the present respondent No.3, respondent No.4, respondent No.5, and respondent No.6 under section 7Ka of the Arbitration Act 2001 before the District Judge, Dhaka, who by its order dated 23-4-2024 in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No.33 of 2024 admitted the above application and also issued show cause notice for 15 days, against which, the petitioner preferred a Civil Revision No.1839 of 2024 before the Hon'ble High Court Division, where in the Rule was issued and also passed an order of ad-interim injunction by restraining to encashment of the Bank Guarantee (Annexures-3, 4, 5 and 6 to the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent No.3). 

 50. It further transpires from Annexure-7 of the affidavit-in-opposition that the petitioner also issued a Notice of Arbitration dated 27-6-2024 to respondent No.4 and respondent No.6. Thereafter, the petitioner, on 30-6-2024, filed the instant Writ Petition No.8220 of 2024 in the High Court Division, challenging the impugned memos. Subsequently, the petitioner has filed another application under section 12 of the Arbitration Act 2001 for the appointment of an arbitrator (in which the respondent No.3 is a pro form arespondent), which is numbered as Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No.407 of 2024 before the learned Court of District Judge, Dhaka. 

 53. The notices concern commercial contracts, for which a writ petition is generally not the appropriate remedy; civil jurisdiction or arbitration would be the proper remedy. The petitioner already has initiated alternative and efficacious remedies and is actively pursuing them through multiple arbitration cases (including Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No.407 of 2024 for arbitrator appointment and Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No.33 of 2024 for ad-interim status quo) and a Civil Revision No. 1839 of 2024. This indicates the matter involves disputed questions of fact best resolved in those forums. 

 54. Given the presented facts, circumstances, and legal decisions from all parties, this court has come to the conclusion that the instant writ petition is not maintainable. As a result, we feel not necessary to delve into the merits of the case. Consequently, the Rule Nisi is liable to be discharged as not being maintainable.
